About: The Electric Dipole — Two Charges That Almost Cancel

Source

Topic
Electrostatics — the electric dipole
Concept
The dipole field is the small residue of two nearly-cancelling charges, and it falls as 1/r³ — doubling the distance divides it by eight, not four.
Serves
Recognise 1/r³ falloff for a dipole; compute axial and equatorial fields; know that Eaxial = 2·Eequatorial far away.
Inquiry
At r = 10 cm the axial field is 734 V/m. What is it at r = 20 cm?
Misconception
"A dipole is just two charges, so its field falls as 1/r² like any charge."

Guided Inquiry

Set the scene

A dipole is a +q and a −q a tiny distance d apart. The star sits on the dipole's own axis, a distance r from the centre — the axial (end-on) position. There the field from +q pushes one way and the field from −q pulls almost the opposite way, so the two faint arrows nearly cancel and only the bold sum is left.

The sidebar reads that axial field, and beside it the equatorial (broadside-on) one — same r, out on the perpendicular bisector.

Predict — the star moves out

At r = 10 cm the axial field is ≈ 734 V/m. Now imagine dragging the sample point out to r = 20 cm — twice as far. What does the field become?

Verify — drag the sample out

Move the Sample distance r slider to 20 cm and read the axial field. You should see it drop to about 90 V/m — an eighth of 734 V/m (exactly ⅛ only in the far-field limit r ≫ d).

Look at the scene: the two faint arrows (E+ from +q, E− from −q) grow almost equal and opposite. The bold sum is what's left over — and it's tiny.

Compare — dipole vs single charge

The right panel now draws a single point charge's 1/r² line next to the dipole's line. Both are straight on log-log axes, but their slopes differ: −2 for the point charge, −3 for the dipole.

That extra factor of 1/r is the mark of the near-cancellation — the dipole's field falls faster than any single charge could.

The standard result

Far from the dipole, the axial field is exactly twice the equatorial field. The sidebar shows both — check the ratio, and drag r outward to watch it settle toward 2.

Eaxial = 2kp/r³, Eequatorial = kp/r³ ⇒ ratio = 2. This factor of two is a standard JEE result.

The Physics

The Electric Dipole — Two Charges That Almost Cancel · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

An electric dipole is a +q and a −q held a short distance d apart. The sim puts a sample point, the star, on the line through the two charges and shows what the pair does to the electric field there.

What you'll learn

  • What the dipole moment p = q·d measures.
  • How the fields of the two charges combine at the star.
  • How the field of the pair depends on the distance r from its centre.
  • How the field on the axis compares with the field broadside to it.
The star sits on the line through both charges, on the +q side.

What's on screen

  • +q, and a faint arrow E+: the field the +q makes at the star.
  • −q, and a faint arrow E−: the field the −q makes at the star.
  • The star and the bold arrow beside it: the sum of the two fields.
  • Field vs distance plot, and a readout panel with the field in V/m.
See itLook at the scene as it opens. Watch for: a red + and a blue − close together, and a star to their right.

03

The dipole moment is the charge times the separation

The pair has no net charge, so what matters is how big the charges are and how far apart they sit. The dipole moment combines both:

p = qd
p in C·m, pointing from −q to +q. In the sim that is along +x.
  • At the start, q = 2.0 nC and d = 2.0 cm, so p = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 0.020 = 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ C·m.
  • Doubling q or doubling d doubles p. Halving d while doubling q leaves p unchanged.
  • The readout panel shows p, and it does not depend on r.
See itKeep q at 2.0 nC and stretch the gap to d = 4.0 cm. Watch for: the dipole moment readout doubling to 8.00e-11 C·m.
04

On the axis the two fields nearly cancel

The star is a distance r from the centre, so it is r − d/2 from the +q and r + d/2 from the −q. The +q makes a field pointing away from it, along +x at the star. The −q makes one pointing toward it, along −x. The two point opposite ways, so they subtract:

Eaxial = kq [ 1/(r − d/2)² − 1/(r + d/2)² ]
The nearer charge wins at the star, so the sum points along +x, the same way as p.
r = 10 cm, d = 2 cm, q = 2 nCdistancefield
E+ from +q9 cm2219 V/m
E− from −q11 cm1486 V/m
sum733.6 V/m

Only about a third of the larger field survives. The closer the charges sit compared with r, the more the two fields cancel.

See itRead the scene at the start values. Watch for: the bold amber arrow much shorter than the red one, and a sum of 733.6 V/m.
05

Far from the dipole the field falls as 1/r³

Put the two terms of Eaxial over one denominator. The numerator is 2kqrd, and when r is much larger than d the denominator is almost r⁴:

Eaxial = 2kqrd / (r² − d²/4)² ≈ 2kp / r³  (r ≫ d)
Doubling r divides the field by 2³ = 8.
q = 2 nC, d = 2 cmexact Eaxial2kp / r³
r = 10 cm733.6 V/m719.0 V/m
r = 20 cm90.33 V/m89.88 V/m

The exact ratio from 10 cm to 20 cm is 8.12, not 8. The shortcut is 2% low at 10 cm and 0.5% low at 20 cm, so it gets better as r grows. A bigger gap needs a bigger r: with d = 5 cm the same ratio is 8.82.

See itSlide r from 10 cm to 20 cm. Watch for: the axial field dropping to 90.33 V/m, about an eighth of its old value.
06

A dipole fades faster than a single charge

A single charge q has E = kq/r², a straight line of slope −2 on a log-log plot. The dipole curve is a line of slope −3 once r is large. The dashed grey line in the plot is the single charge, drawn with the same q.

Dividing the two far-field formulas shows how the gap widens:

Edipole / Esingle ≈ 2d / r
The extra factor of 1/r comes from the near-cancellation.
  • At r = 10 cm the dipole gives 733.6 / 1797.5 = 0.41 of a single charge. The formula gives 2d/r = 0.40.
  • At r = 50 cm it gives 5.757 / 71.90 = 0.080. The formula gives 0.080.
  • Near r = 6 cm the curve is a little steeper than −3, about −3.1 for d = 2 cm.
See itMove the star out to r = 50 cm. Watch for: the teal dipole line far below the dashed grey line, and a field of 5.757 V/m.
07

Far away the axial field is twice the equatorial field

The equatorial point lies on the perpendicular bisector of the pair, at the same distance r from the centre. Each charge is √(r² + d²/4) away. The two fields have equal size, and their parts along the bisector cancel. Only the parts along the axis add:

Eeq = kqd / (r² + d²/4)3/2 ≈ kp / r³  (r ≫ d)
Eeq points opposite to p. The sim shows only its size.

Comparing with 2kp/r³ gives Eaxial / Eeq → 2 for r ≫ d. The readout panel shows the exact ratio:

q = 2 nCEaxialEeqratio
d = 2 cm, r = 10 cm733.6354.22.071
d = 2 cm, r = 50 cm5.7572.8742.003
d = 5 cm, r = 10 cm2045820.62.492
See itMove the star out to r = 50 cm. Watch for: the ratio readout settling at 2.003, very close to 2.
08

Where it matters

  • Polar molecules. In a molecule such as water the charge is not spread evenly, so it has a permanent dipole moment p. Its field far away is a dipole field.
  • Torque. In a uniform field E, a dipole feels no net force. It feels a torque of size pE sin θ, where θ is the angle between p and E. The torque turns p toward E.
  • Energy. The potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field is −p·E. It is lowest when p lies along E.
  • Induced dipoles. An atom or molecule pushed out of shape by an outside field gets a dipole moment of its own, and the field it makes fades as 1/r³.
09

Summary

In one line. A +q and a −q close together almost cancel, and the small field left over depends on the moment p = q·d and on how far away you stand.

Key points

  • p = q·d, pointing from −q to +q.
  • On the axis the two fields subtract, so far away Eaxial ≈ 2kp/r³.
  • Doubling r divides the dipole field by 8. A single charge loses a factor of 4.
  • Eeq ≈ kp/r³, so the axial field is twice the equatorial one for r ≫ d.

Common mix-ups

  • "A dipole is two charges, so its field falls as 1/r²." The two fields nearly cancel, so the sum falls faster than either.
  • "Doubling r always divides E by exactly 8." Only for r ≫ d. At r = 10 cm and d = 2 cm the factor is 8.12.
  • "A dipole has no field because its net charge is zero." The charges sit at different places, so the fields do not cancel exactly.

Things to try on your own

  • Set d = 5 cm and r = 6 cm and see how far the ratio is from 2.
  • Raise q from 0.5 to 5 nC and see which readouts change and which do not.
  • Find how large r must be for the ratio to read below 2.01 with d = 2 cm.
